paragraphs.source_en: Depending on a person's profession, this rush of blood to the head is a matter of great importance; there are some people who can do nothing at all unless it comes over them. Among them, the ones who prize this rush of blood most highly are poets. A poet needs such excitement just as a steamship cannot do without coal; if a poet does not have it, he degenerates into an idle common fellow capable of nothing but eating his meals. Of course, a rush of blood to the head is only another name for madness; yet since it would sound quite bad in public to say that they cannot make a living unless they go mad, poets do not call it by that name among themselves, but have all agreed to refer to it, in a most solemn and mysterious fashion, as “inspiration.” This is a term they manufactured to deceive society; in truth it is simply a rush of blood to the head. Plato, taking their side, called this kind of excitement “divine madness”; but however divine it may be, if it is madness people will have nothing to do with them, so I think it is probably better for their sake to give it a name like some newly invented patent medicine. But just as the main ingredient of fish cake is yam, as a carved image of Kannon is originally a piece of rotten wood an inch and eight-tenths long, as the duck soba is made with crow meat, and as the boarding-house beef hotpot uses horse meat, so “inspiration” is in fact a rush of blood to the head. Since it is a rush of blood to the head, it ought to be called a temporary madness. There is no need to send this condition to the asylum at Sugamo, because it is only a temporary madness. The trouble is that manufacturing this temporary madness is no easy matter. A lifelong lunatic is, if anything, easy to produce; but to make a man go mad only while he takes up his brush and faces the paper seems to be a task even the most skillful deity finds rather taxing, and such a specimen is not readily made. Since God will not make one for us, we have no choice but to make one by our own efforts. For this reason, from ancient times down to the present day, the search for methods of producing or removing this rush of blood has troubled scholars just as much. Some people, in order to obtain “inspiration,” have eaten twelve astringent persimmons every day; this follows from the theory that eating astringent persimmons causes constipation, and constipation is sure to bring on a rush of blood to the head. Another person took a warmed flask of sake and jumped into a bath, thinking that if he drank a few cups in hot water, a rush of blood was bound to occur. According to this man's theory, if that method failed, he was convinced that heating a whole bathful of wine and climbing into it would produce an immediate effect. Unfortunately, the man was penniless, and so he died without ever being able to put the experiment into practice. Finally, there was someone who thought that inspiration would arise if he imitated the ancients; this was an application of the theory that when one imitates another person's attitude and movements, the imitator's mental state comes to resemble that person's. That is to say, if one keeps rambling on like a drunkard, before one knows it one comes to feel as if one has been drinking. If a person practicing Zen endures patiently until one stick of incense has burned down, he too will feel as though he has truly become a Zen monk.

paragraphs.source_zh: 根据人的职业不同，虚火上升还是非常重要的，有的人如果虚火不上升就什么事也干不成。其中最重视虚火上升的是诗人。诗人必须虚火上升就和轮船不能缺煤一样，诗人如果虚火不上升，那他只能堕落为无所事事的、除了吃饭之外一无所能的凡夫俗子。当然，虚火上升也就是疯子的别名，既然他们不成为疯子就无法混饭吃，而在舆论上又未免太难听，所以在诗人当中，并不以虚火上升来称呼它，而一致同意神乎其神地称之为“烟士比里纯”。这是他们为欺骗社会制造的称呼，其实就是虚火上升。柏拉图为了吹捧他们，将这种虚火上升称之为“神圣的疯癫”，不管如何神圣，既然是疯癫，人们就不会搭理他们，所以我想，还是加给它这样一个类似新发明的成药的名字，这样对他们也许会有好处。但是，正像鱼糕的主料是山芋、雕出来的观音像原是一段一寸八分的朽木头、鸭肉面使用的材料是老鸹肉、公寓里的牛肉锅用的是马肉一样，“烟士比里纯”其实就是虚火上升。从虚火上升这个词儿来看，应该说是一时的疯癫。虚火上升毋需送入巢鸭的疯人院，因为它只是短期疯癫罢了。不过，要使自己短期疯癫不是件容易的事。一辈子的疯子不难找到，但要找一个面对稿纸一握起笔来就临时发疯的人，这对万能的神来说，似乎也相当费力，轻易造不出一个来。既然神造不出来，那就只能自己动手来制造啦。正因为如此，所以自古以来直到今天，寻找虚火上升或者下降的办法，同样伤透了学者的脑筋。有的人为了获得“烟士比里纯”，每天要吃十二个涩柿子，这是从“吃了涩柿子就会便秘，便秘了肯定会虚火上升”这一理论推论而来的。同时，也有的人拿着烫好了的一壶酒跳进浴缸里，以为在热水中喝上几口酒肯定会虚火上升。根据此人说法，如果此法还不灵，他相信只要烧上一澡盆葡萄酒，跳进去便能立见功效。可惜那人是个穷光蛋，所以始终未能付诸实施，就一命归天了。最后还有一种人，想到只要模仿古人就能产生“烟士比里纯”，这是应用这样一种学说：只要模仿某人的态度和动作，模仿者的心态就和那人相似起来。也就是说，模仿喝醉酒的人那样唠唠叨叨个没完，模仿不知不觉也就觉得仿佛是喝醉了一般。参禅的人，在一炷香燃尽之前，耐住性子，也会觉得自己仿佛真成了禅和尚。

paragraphs.source_en: Therefore, if one imitates the every gesture and action of some famous master who long ago received inspiration, one is certain to become flushed with excitement. As I understand it, Hugo lay on a swift boat while pondering the design of his prose, so if one merely sits in a boat and fixes one's eyes on the blue sky, a rush of blood is guaranteed. Stevenson, they say, wrote novels lying flat on his stomach; therefore, if one lies prone and takes up one's pen, the blood is sure to rise upside down. In this way, all sorts of people have devised all sorts of methods, but no one has yet succeeded. For the present, artificial excitement has become an impossibility; it is regrettable, but there is nothing to be done. Of course, the time when inspiration can be produced at will is bound to arrive sooner or later. For the sake of the advancement of human culture, I earnestly hope that this time will come as soon as possible.
